questions.q: Of the seas the Court names for central and southern Italy, which one washes the eastern coast of the Marche, Abruzzo and northern Puglia?
questions.exp: The Adriatic runs down the eastern coast from the Marche through Abruzzo and Molise to Puglia, while the Tyrrhenian lies off Lazio, Campania and Calabria to the west and the Ligurian Sea further north; the Court names all three with Vesuvius.

questions.q: The Court says a young Sagrantino di Montefalco should be decanted. Which young Campanian red does it pair with Sagrantino in that advice?
questions.exp: Young Taurasi, Aglianico from the Irpinian hills, and young Sagrantino di Montefalco are two of Italy's most tannic reds, and the Court advises decanting both so that air can soften their grip before they reach the glass.

questions.q: Which region of central Italy is landlocked, lying between Tuscany and the Marche?
questions.exp: Umbria is the only Italian region with neither a coastline nor a foreign border, and it is home to Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG; Lazio, Abruzzo and Molise all reach the sea, part of the map the Court asks a candidate to know.

questions.q: Which climate category does the Court give the inland hills of central Italy, away from the coast?
questions.exp: The Court reads central Italy as maritime on the coast and continental inland, where the Apennines cut off the sea's influence and bring colder winters and wider swings between day and night; it gives the south a Mediterranean climate.

questions.q: Which soil type does the Court give for Campania, home of Taurasi, Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo?
questions.exp: Campania's soils are volcanic, ash, tuff and lava from Vesuvius, the Campi Flegrei and Roccamonfina, the Court's one word for the region, and the Irpinian DOCGs mix volcanic ash with clay and limestone; galestro is Tuscan, chalk belongs to Champagne and slate to the Mosel.
